Analysis: It quantitatively shows tiny denominators drive collapse, uses t-SNE to reveal divergence between prefixed/unprefixed key distributions specifically for first tokens, and triangulates with tokenizer-start effects (s in Llama2) and a T5 encoder counterexample. Experiment: Rigorous evaluations on COUNTERFACT/HardCF and ME-PPL50 across GPT-2-XL, GPT-J, and Llama2-7b compare the original ROME vs C-ROME and the added test-time prefixing; metrics include perplexity, efficacy, generalization, and locality. Results: C-ROME eliminates collapse (ME-PPL remains close to original) and preserves locality; adding test-time prefixes restores high efficacy on collapse cases (100% for GPT-2-XL/J), confirming the causal link and practical effectiveness of the proposed fixes.

Experiments rigorously compare Original ROME, C-ROME (consistent keys), and C-ROME + test-time prefixing on COUNTERFACT/HardCF across GPT-2-XL, GPT-J, and Llama2-7b, separating collapse vs. normal subsets. Metrics include ME-PPL50 for collapse severity and standard editing metrics (efficacy, generalization, locality). Results: ROME collapses with extreme ME-PPL50 (GPT-2-XL 26,084.66; GPT-J 25,909.24; Llama2-7b 10,574.76) versus original perplexities (~68.77/49.04/33.18). C-ROME restores stability (collapse cases: 70.71/51.77/33.20; normal cases near original). Without prefixing, C-ROME’s efficacy/generalization on collapse cases is low (efficacy: 5.19%/30.59%/18.65%; generalization: 14.29%/30.77%/12.70%) while maintaining high locality (97.40%/82.35%/100%). Adding test-time prefixes recovers collapse-case efficacy (100%/100%/12.70%) and preserves high locality (100%/89.41%/100%), with limited generalization gains (16.88%/32.94%/12.70%) and minimal regressions on normal cases (e.g., GPT-2-XL normal: 96.16%/41.88%/97.34%).

Insightful analysis ties collapse to the anomalous distribution of first-token representations in autoregressive decoders, explaining why unprefixed keys diverge from prefixed ones specifically when the subject is first. The role of tokenizer start tokens (s in Llama2) and a T5 encoder counterexample strengthen the causal narrative from distribution shift to a vanishing denominator.

Weaknesses: Experimental coverage is narrow: primary analyses center on GPT-2-XL and GPT-J, with limited exploration of larger or more diverse LLMs and only cursory treatment of Llama2-7b. Evidence: the paper’s Limitations explicitly note the focus on GPT-2-XL/GPT-J; for Llama2-7b, collapse cases are rare (21/21,919) and their specific characteristics remain unknown, with behavior tied to the s tokenizer (Sec. 3.3; App. A.3). Evaluations are conducted on COUNTERFACT/HardCF using ME-PPL50 (Tables 2 and 4) plus efficacy/generalization/locality (Tables 3 and 4), without additional datasets. Sequential editing is out of scope and deferred (Limitations). The method uses “a small set of N randomly sampled prefixes” for k* and test-time random prefixes, but no sensitivity analyses over N or prefix length/content are reported. Distributional evidence relies on t-SNE visualizations (Figs. 1–2) rather than formal statistical tests of distance or separation.

Novelty is modest: the inconsistent-key issue was identified concurrently by other work, and the proposed fixes (key consistency and test-time prefixing) are straightforward. The paper lacks head-to-head comparisons with alternative editing/stabilization methods (e.g., MEMIT, ROME variants, causal patching/gradient-based editors), making it hard to assess relative advantage.

Results and experiments indicate limited editing quality despite preventing collapse. Without test-time prefixing, C-ROME’s efficacy and generalization on collapse cases are very low (e.g., Table 3: GPT-2-XL efficacy 5.19%, generalization 14.29%; GPT-J efficacy 30.59%, generalization 30.77%; Llama2-7b efficacy 18.65%), and even with prefixing, generalization remains weak (Table 4: 16.88% for GPT-2-XL, 32.94% for GPT-J) while Llama2-7b efficacy is only 12.70%. The experimental evidence for the first-token mechanism relies heavily on t-SNE visualizations and descriptive observations; there are no quantitative distributional tests (e.g., cosine distance statistics, KS tests), effect sizes, or confidence intervals, and no ablations on prefix length/content or number of prefixes to stress-test robustness. Conclusions for Llama2-7b are further limited by the very small number of collapse cases (~21/21,919), making the reported results hard to generalize. Overall, the analysis supports the denominator issue qualitatively, but the result quality and experimental rigor are insufficient to substantiate stronger claims about efficacy and generalization.

7) Practicality: training 1k+ per-head preliminary probes for head selection may be costly for larger models; scalability not fully addressed.

6) Computational overhead and complexity: added modules and augmented data increase training time; no detailed runtime/memory analysis beyond a brief note.
7) Reporting: few contemporary generative baselines, no significance testing, and limited variance reporting.

1.llm_review: Methodology is clearly defined and well-executed, with thorough description and interpretation. IntCoOp learns attribute-level inductive biases by (i) generating per-image attribute labels offline via a BLIP-2 VQA pipeline, (ii) training a lightweight attribute extractor A that maps CLIP vision features V(I) to an attribute embedding, and (iii) inserting this embedding into the prompt alongside instance-conditioned context tokens produced by multi-head attention over V(I). Deep visual prompting enriches frozen CLIP features by appending learnable tokens to ViT layers up to depth K, and a regularization term aligns learned prompts with a diverse set of attribute-rich templates. The overall loss L = LCE + λ1 Lattr + λ2 Lreg is well-motivated: it couples class alignment, attribute supervision, and prompt regularity. This design is interpretable—attributes are explicit components of the prompt—and the paper explains why aligning compositional attributes with class tokens should improve generalization and robustness while keeping the backbone frozen.

The total objective L = LCE + λ1 Lattr + λ2 Lreg is well-motivated: LCE enforces class alignment, Lattr ensures attribute faithfulness, and Lreg curbs overfitting. Deep visual prompting enriches V(I) by appending n learnable tokens up to depth K, and a regularization term aligns learned prompts with a diverse pool of attribute-rich templates. The total objective L = LCE + λ1 Lattr + λ2 Lreg is well-motivated: LCE enforces class alignment, Lattr ensures attribute faithfulness, and Lreg curbs overfitting. The paper clearly explains why explicit attribute tokens and attention-based conditioning improve compositional alignment, generalization, and interpretability while keeping CLIP backbones frozen.

Methodologically solid architecture: a lightweight attribute extractor (hypernetwork) trained with Lattr, instance-conditioned context via multi-head attention, deep visual prompting to enrich frozen CLIP features, and a regularization loss toward a diverse pool of attribute-rich templates. Evidence: (1) Attribute extractor A is explicitly a compact two-layer network with ReLU trained via Lattr = ||A(V(I)) − T(aI)|| (Eq. 4), with f=2 (Sec. 4.1). (2) Instance conditioning uses a Multi-Head Attention module h(I) = MultiHead(Query=u, Key=V(I), Value=V(I)) and composes prompts p+(I) = [h1,…,hM, A(V(I)), [cls]c] (Eq. 5, Sec. 4.2). (3) Deep visual prompting appends n learnable visual tokens {Zi} up to depth K in the CLIP vision transformer to produce richer representations for A; ablations in Table 3 show K=9 outperforms shallow prompting (Sec. 4.1, Table 3). (4) Prompt regularization aligns learned prompts to a pool of N=80 attribute-enriched templates (Lreg, Eq. 6, Sec. 4.3). (5) The approach targets CLIP-like models without modifying encoder weights, learning only added tokens and small heads, and is stated to be easily applicable to a broad family of CLIP-style models (Sec. 4).

Strong experimental support for the method: across 10 datasets in base-to-novel generalization and multiple domain-shift benchmarks, IntCoOp consistently outperforms prior prompt-tuning approaches (e.g., +1.27% HM over LFA in 16-shot) and shows improved robustness. Ablations substantiate design choices (deep visual prompting and attention-based conditioning).

Weaknesses: Contribution is incremental: while integrating attribute-level cues into prompt tuning is useful, the conceptual novelty over CoCoOp/MaPLe/VPT-style conditioning and prompt regularization is moderate, and average gains over the strongest baselines are relatively small. Evidence: (i) The approach primarily recombines known elements—instance-conditioned prompts via attention (Section 4.2), which parallels CoCoOp-style image conditioning; deep visual prompting by appending learnable visual tokens to CLIP layers (Section 4.1), akin to VPT; and regularization toward a pool of textual templates (Section 4.3), conceptually related to KgCoOp’s knowledge-guided regularization. (ii) The reported margins are modest on average: in base-to-novel generalization (16-shot), IntCoOp reaches 80.75 HM vs 79.48 for LFA (Table 1; +1.27 pp); in domain generalization, IntCoOp averages 60.71 vs 60.28 (MaPLe), 60.27 (RPO), and 60.19 (LASP) (Table 2; ≤0.52 pp over strong baselines). Although certain datasets (e.g., EuroSAT) show larger gains, the cross-dataset averages remain small.

Comparison, Embeddings, and Performance: (1) Comparison: The main results rely on authors’ re-implementations on CLIP ViT-B/16, and several baselines (e.g., PLOT, ProGrad) are known to be sensitive to tuning; the unusually low PLOT numbers and absence of official or strongly tuned baselines raise fairness concerns. Broader comparisons across backbones (e.g., ViT-L/14) and shot regimes should be in the main text, alongside significance testing, to substantiate comparative claims. (2) Embeddings: The method’s gains hinge on attribute embeddings supervised by BLIP-2; potential noise/bias in these pseudo-labels is not quantified, and there is limited analysis of how deep visual prompting and the attribute extractor alter or drift CLIP’s representation space. More probing of embedding quality and stability (beyond cosine similarity) is needed. (3) Performance: Average improvements over strong prompt-tuning baselines are modest (e.g., +1.27% HM over LFA at 16-shot; small margins in domain generalization vs MaPLe/RPO/LASP), and no variances/confidence intervals are reported, making statistical significance unclear. The large reported gap over PLOT appears driven by that method’s low scores, further underscoring the need for stronger, fairer comparisons.

Ablation and results are not sufficiently validated. On the ablation side, Table 3 only contrasts shallow vs deep visual prompting and additive vs attention-based conditioning, but does not isolate the contribution of core losses/components (e.g., removing Lattr or Lreg, or replacing the attribute extractor with a null/identity head) to show where gains come from. There is no sensitivity study for key hyperparameters (λ1/λ2, context length M, number/placement of visual tokens n/K, number of synthetic prompts N, attention heads), leaving it unclear how brittle the method is. Although one “attribute swap” test is provided, robustness to graded noise levels or partial attribute availability is not explored. On the results side, average gains over strong baselines are modest (e.g., ~+1.27% HM over LFA in 16-shot) and vary by dataset; the paper reports means over 3 seeds but lacks standard deviations/confidence intervals or statistical tests, making it hard to assess significance. Generality across backbones is not demonstrated (all main results on CLIP ViT-B/16), and per-dataset analyses suggest improvements concentrate on attribute-rich domains without showing consistent benefits elsewhere. Adding comprehensive component ablations, hyperparameter sensitivity, robustness curves for attribute noise, variance reporting, and results on additional CLIP backbones would substantiate the claims.

502_aggregate.e2e_review:
Strengths: - Presents a clear, model-agnostic framework (TWIST) that reuses LoRA weight increments via a reusable weight pool, with a principled dual-stage pipeline for preparation and optimization.
- Novel multi-key memory retrieval that combines task- and instance-level signals; adaptive retrieval improves relevance of transferred weights.
- SVD-based merging of LoRA matrices to mitigate parameter interference; thorough ablations and q-sensitivity analyses support design choices.
- Strong empirical gains in low-resource settings across diverse styles; competitive results on large backbones (LLaMA2-7B) and close to GPT-4 few-shot on style accuracy; human evaluation indicates better content preservation.
- Broad experimental coverage: multiple datasets (sentiment, formality, writing, role-specific dialogue), two backbone families, scaling analyses, and qualitative visualizations.

Weaknesses: 1) Evaluation metrics: content preservation relies on Self-BLEU; lacks semantic similarity measures (e.g., BERTScore/BLURT/SemSim). Style accuracy uses in-domain classifiers without calibration or robustness checks; human evaluation is small-scale with no inter-annotator agreement reported.
2) Baselines: comparisons on T5 lean on older methods; missing recent strong TST and controllable generation baselines (e.g., diffusion/editing/plug-and-play/modern LLM editing), and parameter-merging baselines tuned for generation. LLaMA comparisons omit strong open fine-tuned instruction models beyond QLoRA.
3) Claims vs results: not consistently SOTA (e.g., underperforms B-GST on formality). No statistical significance tests.
4) Method clarity: details of clustering (number of clusters), key optimization (K, masking rate), lambda/q selection, and sensitivity are only partially explored; the task-level query design and per-task instantiation could be clearer to rule out leakage or overfitting.
5) Efficiency/practicality: retrieval and memory overhead not quantified in the main text (latency, memory footprint); trade-offs vs simply fine-tuning LoRA with few shots are not fully characterized.
6) Generalization limits: English-only; reliance on frozen BERT for queries may not transfer across languages or domains.
7) Reproducibility: code/weights not provided; classifier training details and prompts are partially relegated to appendices.

521_aggregate.e2e_review:
Strengths: • Proposes a unified, multi-criteria active retrieval framework (intent-, knowledge-, time-, and self-aware) that casts each criterion as a plug-and-play classifier on frozen LLM hidden states, avoiding full-model finetuning and adding negligible overhead.
• Introduces a standardized decision policy (UAR-Criteria) to combine criteria, enabling consistent retrieval timing across diverse scenarios.
• Curates AR-Bench covering four orthogonal active-retrieval subtasks; evaluates comprehensively on AR-Bench and six downstream datasets (knowledge-, time-, and self-aware scenarios) with 7B/13B Llama2-chat.
• Demonstrates consistent overall gains vs FLARE, Self-RAG, and SKR on both AR-Bench and downstream tasks; analysis includes ablations (single classifiers vs composed policy, value head vs whole LLM) and document-number sensitivity.
• Practical contribution: simple to integrate, minimal inference cost, and code/data release promised.

Weaknesses: 1) Intent-aware evidence is limited: the intent data are synthetic (Self-Instruct seeded by 10 intents) and there is no downstream evaluation that quantifies its real utility; generalization to real user intents is unclear.
2) Evaluation relies on ChatGPT for TAQA/FreshQA without inter-annotator checks or robustness analysis; no statistical significance testing is reported.
3) Baseline comparability is imperfect: Self-RAG is fine-tuned on base models while others use chat models; FLARE/SKR are re-implemented and may be suboptimal; several recent active-retrieval/uncertainty baselines are missing.
4) The decision-tree ordering is heuristic and untested; cascading errors likely. Per-scenario single classifiers outperform the composed UAR policy on their own tasks, and the self-aware head is a notable bottleneck (~72–76% accuracy).
5) Claims of negligible overhead and improved efficiency lack end-to-end runtime/latency and cost measurements; retrieval frequency is reported but not wall-clock gains.
6) Data construction risks: self-aware labels from multiple generations can be noisy; AR-Bench is balanced and draws from related sources, which may not reflect real-world distributions.
7) Scope limited to short-form, single-call retrieval; multi-hop/long-form scenarios are not evaluated.
8) Improvements on some datasets are modest; it is unclear if differences are statistically significant.

Strengths: - Addresses an important, underexplored NLP-for-social-good problem (destigmatizing substance use language) with clear motivation and social relevance.
- Introduces a multi-stage computational framework grounded in a well-established stigma theory (Link and Phelan), with an explanation layer for detected stigma.
- Creates and plans to release a sizable dataset of stigmatizing posts and paired destigmatized rewrites from non-drug-related subreddits, enabling future research.
- Proposes an informed + stylistic LLM prompting approach that preserves emotional tone and style (via GoEmotions, syntax, MTLD) while reducing stigma.
- Provides both human and automatic evaluations; human reviewers prefer the informed + stylized GPT-4 system for overall quality and faithfulness; LIWC indicates psycholinguistic similarity is largely preserved.
- Offers descriptive analyses (topics, entities, emotions) that yield insights into how stigma manifests across substances and interpersonal contexts.

Weaknesses: 1) Heavy reliance on proprietary LLMs for filtering and labeling with limited human gold. Stigma detection beyond a small annotated set (kappa=0.67 on 200) lacks thorough quantitative validation (no precision/recall for stigma and attributes), risking label bias and circularity.
2) Human evaluation is modest (5 reviewers, 110 posts) and rank-based without statistical tests; reviewers are not target stakeholders (e.g., people with lived experience, clinicians). No validated stigma-reduction scales are used.
3) Clarity and consistency issues: mismatched counts for directed stigma vs. destigmatized pairs; some tables and methodological details are incomplete or relegated to appendices; Constitutional AI is loosely characterized.
4) Limited baselines and ablations: no comparison to established detoxification or rule-based person-first rewriting; no ablation of stylistic components to isolate their contribution.
5) Automatic evaluation is narrow: LIWC multiple-comparison concerns, no objective semantic faithfulness or content-preservation metrics; potential meaning drift is insufficiently quantified.
6) External validity is limited (English, four non-drug subreddits). Ethical considerations of rewriting user content and potential misrepresentation are only briefly discussed.
7) No downstream impact evaluation: does the rewritten text measurably reduce stigmatizing perceptions or improve supportive engagement in user studies?
589_aggregate.collab_review:
Strengths: Analysis, Data, Model: The paper offers a well-instrumented pipeline grounded in rigorous analysis, a substantial dataset, and a principled modeling setup. Data: It curates 1.51M posts from four non–drug-related subreddits, filters 33,064 drug-mention posts (GPT-3.5), validates 16,277 (GPT-4), and identifies 3,207 stigmatizing instances (1,949 directed), culminating in 1,649 de-stigmatized pairs slated for release—providing a valuable resource with transparent preprocessing and labeling stages. Model: The stigma detection and rewriting are explicitly guided by Link & Phelan’s taxonomy (labeling, stereotyping, separation, discrimination), with explainable outputs for detection and a three-tier rewriting approach (baseline → informed → informed+stylized). The best-performing system (Informed+Stylized GPT-4) integrates few-shot exemplars plus stylistic controls (emotion via GoEmotions-RoBERTa, sentence structure, MTLD, passive voice), achieving top human ratings for overall quality and faithfulness. Analysis: The study triangulates BERTopic/KeyBERT topic modeling, subject–verb/entity analyses, and emotion profiling to surface key patterns (e.g., stigma clustered around stimulants and cannabis, interpersonal/familial contexts). A LIWC-based t-test shows psycholinguistic similarity between originals and rewrites, supporting the claim that style and tone are preserved while stigma is reduced.

The paper addresses an important, underexplored problem with clear practical implications and offers a concrete toolchain for moderating/rewriting stigmatizing content while preserving tone, which could benefit both research and deployment settings.

Weaknesses: Generalization is limited: the corpus is drawn from four English, non–drug-related subreddits, yielding few structural-stigma cases and a Reddit-specific style profile; there is no out-of-domain testing (other subreddits, platforms, time periods, or languages), no cross-cultural analysis (where stigma norms and person-first conventions differ), and no robustness checks to domain shift (e.g., different substance mixes or community norms). The evaluation (110 posts, 5 reviewers) does not establish external validity, and reliance on English-centric tools (GoEmotions, LIWC) further constrains transferability.

Annotation is a key weakness: the manual gold set is very small and under-specified. Only 200 posts were annotated to seed stigma labels (κ≈0.67 overall), with no per-category κ for labeling/stereotyping/separation/discrimination, no class-wise confusion analysis, and no clear adjudication protocol. Annotator expertise in SUD stigma, training materials, and codebook boundaries are not described beyond brief mentions, making it hard to assess consistency on subtle cases (e.g., moral judgment vs. discrimination). The remainder of the corpus is auto-labeled by GPT-4 using the same taxonomy, but there is no sizable, stratified human audit of these labels, nor error rates reported per attribute; this risks propagating model biases and rationalization errors from the explanation layer. For the 1,649 de-stigmatized pairs, the acceptance/QA criteria and any human verification are unclear. Please expand and document the gold annotations (stratified by subreddit and stigma type), report per-attribute agreement, use adjudication with a detailed codebook, and conduct a larger, blinded audit of GPT-4 labels to calibrate precision/recall before scaling.

Evaluation is limited: small human study (5 reviewers, 110 posts) with rankings only, no inter-rater agreement or statistical tests; no user-centric or real-world impact assessment of reduced stigma; and no comparisons against strong detoxification/rewriting baselines (e.g., person-first lexical substitution, supervised detoxifiers). Automatic evaluation via LIWC is coarse, lacks multiple-comparison controls, and does not directly measure harm reduction or content fidelity beyond style proxies.
